Quadratic graphs · equations · turning points · real-world applications

Formulas & algebraic identities
  • Distributive: a(b+c)=ab+ac, ab+ac=a(b+c); ab+cb=b(a+c).
  • Perfect square addition: (a+b)²=a²+2ab+b².
  • Perfect square subtraction: (a−b)²=a²−2ab+b².
  • Difference of squares: a²−b²=(a+b)(a−b).
  • Zero-product: (A)(B)=0 ⇒ A=0 or B=0.
  • Completing square: x²+bx+c=(x+b/2)²+c−b²/4.
  • Quadratic formula: x=[−b±√(b²−4ac)]/(2a) for ax²+bx+c=0 and a≠0.
  • Roots sum/product: r₁+r₂=−b/a, r₁r₂=c/a.
Graph essentials

For y=ax²+bx+c: a>0 parabola up and minimum; a<0 parabola down and maximum. Smaller |a| means wider graph. Changing c alone translates vertically. Line of symmetry x=−b/(2a). Turning point (−b/(2a), f(−b/(2a))). x-intercepts are solutions with y=0, y-intercept is (0,c). A parabola has 0/1/2 real x-intercepts and exactly one y-intercept.

Nine separate GN textbook image references: 1. Basic y=x² and y=−x²; 2. effect of a; 3. effect of c plus six-function investigation table; 4. general quadratic graph properties; 5. intercepts of y=x²+3x−10, roots −5,2 and y-intercept (0,−10); 6. drawing y=x²+2x+2, x=−3 gives y=5, vertex (−1,1); 7. graph y=7+5x−2x², maximum (1.25,10.125), graph estimate ≈10.2; 8. worked graph and readings; 9. projectile study example y=45t−5t², 5 s height 100 m, ground again at 9 s.

From graph to equation

Vertex form y=a(x−h)²+k if turning point (h,k) and extra point known. Example vertex (2,−3), point (4,5) → a=2 → y=2(x−2)²−3.

Intercept form y=a(x−p)(x−q) if roots p,q and another point known. Example roots −1,3; y-intercept (0,−6) → a=2 → y=2(x+1)(x−3).

Standard form y=ax²+bx+c if three points supplied; substitute to solve coefficient equations. Slides: 1–2 overview/forms; 3–5 vertex; 6–8 intercept; 9–10 standard and a; 11 selection; 12 review; 13 image sources.

Special range rule: If parabola opens up, vertex is minimum globally, but a question asking maximum on a restricted domain requires comparing both endpoints. For y=n, show both algebraic roots and distinguish which lie inside the displayed domain.

Equation methods
  1. Rearrange to ax²+bx+c=0 and simplify denominators.
  2. If already a product, use zero-product.
  3. For a²−b² use difference of squares; for a²±2ab+b² use perfect square.
  4. Otherwise factorise by AC/middle splitting. If not convenient, use square roots, completing square or quadratic formula.
  5. In a 'hence' question, substitute a whole expression for the variable, and reuse the previous factorisation.
  6. Give all valid real roots; reject negative lengths/times as applicable. Δ=b²−4ac: negative means no real roots.
Worked patterns
  • Fraction: 3z²/2−5z+4=0 → multiply by 2 → 3z²−10z+8=0 → (3z−4)(z−2)=0 → z=4/3,2.
  • Identity: (7x−2)²=9 → (7x−2)²−3²=0 → (7x−5)(7x+1)=0 → x=5/7,−1/7.
  • Hence: 10(x−1)²+53(x−1)+36=0 → set u=x−1; (5u+4)(2u+9)=0 → x=1/5,−7/2.
  • Complete square: x²−7x+8=(x−7/2)²−17/4; roots (7±√17)/2.
Linear graphs & coordinates

The user's recorded syllabus also includes these curriculum targets (not all have matching question pages in the three Review Exercise PDFs):

  • Recognise graphs parallel to coordinate axes: x=k and y=k; plot y=x, y=−x.
  • Plot linear graphs using x/y tables.
  • Midpoint of points (x₁,y₁),(x₂,y₂) = ((x₁+x₂)/2,(y₁+y₂)/2).
  • Calculate gradient (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁) and y-intercept of y=mx+c; rearrange ax+by=c when b≠0.
  • Compare rate of change and y-intercepts; interpret straight-line context, distance–time and conversion graphs.
  • Plot two linear equations on common axes; intersection solves simultaneous equations; verify by substitution into both.
  • Quadratic/linear cross-intersections: for a given quadratic y=f(x) and line y=g(x), solve f(x)=g(x) to determine x-values; graph solutions can be approximate.

Existing base-graph method: keep y=x²+2x unchanged and add a comparison line. x²+2x−3=0: graph y=3 intersects at x=−3,1. x²+3x=0: graph y=−x intersects at x=−3,0.

# CONTENT 1 — Algebraic Identities & Laws

## Essential identities

- Distributive: `a(b+c)=ab+ac`, `ab+ac=a(b+c)`; `ab+cb=b(a+c)`.
- Perfect square addition: `(a+b)²=a²+2ab+b²`.
- Perfect square subtraction: `(a−b)²=a²−2ab+b²`.
- Difference of squares: `a²−b²=(a+b)(a−b)`.
- Zero-product: `(A)(B)=0` ⇒ `A=0` **or** `B=0`.
- Completing square: `x²+bx+c=(x+b/2)²+c−b²/4`.
- Quadratic formula: `x=[−b±√(b²−4ac)]/(2a)` for `ax²+bx+c=0` and `a≠0`.
- Roots sum/product: `r₁+r₂=−b/a`, `r₁r₂=c/a`.

# CONTENT 2 — Quadratic Equation Solving (A–1 and B–2/B–3)

## Method selection

1. Rearrange to `ax²+bx+c=0` and simplify denominators.
2. If already a product, use zero-product.
3. For `a²−b²` use difference of squares; for `a²±2ab+b²` use perfect square.
4. Otherwise factorise by AC/middle splitting. If not convenient, use square roots, completing square or quadratic formula.
5. In a 'hence' question, substitute a whole expression for the variable, and reuse the previous factorisation.
6. Give all valid real roots; reject negative lengths/times as applicable. `Δ=b²−4ac`: negative means no real roots.

### Four worked patterns

- **Fraction:** `3z²/2−5z+4=0` → multiply by 2 → `3z²−10z+8=0` → `(3z−4)(z−2)=0` → `z=4/3,2`.
- **Identity:** `(7x−2)²=9` → `(7x−2)²−3²=0` → `(7x−5)(7x+1)=0` → `x=5/7,−1/7`.
- **Hence:** `10(x−1)²+53(x−1)+36=0` → set `u=x−1`; `(5u+4)(2u+9)=0` → `x=1/5,−7/2`.
- **Complete square:** `x²−7x+8=(x−7/2)²−17/4`; roots `(7±√17)/2`.

# CONTENT 3 — Coordinates, Graph Features, Maximum & Minimum

## General rules and graph study data GN

For `y=ax²+bx+c`: `a>0` parabola up and **minimum**; `a<0` parabola down and **maximum**. Smaller `|a|` means wider graph. Changing c alone translates vertically. Line of symmetry `x=−b/(2a)`. Turning point `(−b/(2a), f(−b/(2a)))`. x-intercepts are solutions with `y=0`, y-intercept is `(0,c)`. A parabola has 0/1/2 real x-intercepts and exactly one y-intercept.

**Nine separate GN textbook image references:** 1. Basic `y=x²` and `y=−x²`; 2. effect of `a`; 3. effect of `c` plus six-function investigation table; 4. general quadratic graph properties; 5. intercepts of `y=x²+3x−10`, roots −5,2 and y-intercept (0,−10); 6. drawing `y=x²+2x+2`, x=−3 gives y=5, vertex (−1,1); 7. graph `y=7+5x−2x²`, maximum (1.25,10.125), graph estimate ≈10.2; 8. worked graph and readings; 9. projectile study example `y=45t−5t²`, 5 s height 100 m, ground again at 9 s.

Intercept form `y=a(x−p)(x−q)` if roots p,q and another point known. Example roots −1,3; y-intercept (0,−6) → a=2 → `y=2(x+1)(x−3)`.

## Challenge Yourself (p.130)

1. `(x−2)²+(x+3)²=0`, x real: **no real solution** (two nonnegative squares cannot simultaneously vanish, since x cannot be both 2 and −3).
2. All integer solutions to `x²+y²=10`: `(±1,±3)` and `(±3,±1)`, all sign combinations, **8 ordered pairs**.
3. Solutions to `2x²−6x−k=0` have difference 0: `b²−4ac=36+8k=0`→**k=−9/2**.
4. Roots α,β of `ax²+bx+c=0`: **α+β=−b/a**, **αβ=c/a**. For `2x²+10x+7=0` and p>q: `(p−q)²=(−5)²−4(7/2)=11`→**p−q=√11**.

# CONTENT 7 — Part B–3 Review Exercise 5 WORKBOOK (pp.79–82)

The workbook's Review Exercise 5 starts on p.79; preceding Worksheet 5B and following Worksheet 6A are separate. **Correction priority: follow scanned source and the user's later sharp images, not old draft replies.**

## B3-Q1 Curve through coordinates

Given `y=x²+bx+c` passes `(−1,8)` and `(3,−4)`.

`8=1−b+c` → `−b+c=7` (1); `−4=9+3b+c` → `3b+c=−13` (2). Subtract (1) from (2): `4b=−20`, hence **b=−5**. Substitute: `5+c=7` → **c=2**. Equation `y=x²−5x+2`; **y-intercept (0,2)**. `CLASS: Solve; Algebra Based; Coordinates / Simultaneous Coefficients`.

## B3-Q2 Solve four equations (source checked)

| ID | Original equation | Calculation and correct answer |
|---|---|---|
| B3-2(a) | `86x²=0` | **x=0**. Earlier transcript had 36, but actual workbook reads 86. |
| B3-2(b) | `3−x²/27=0` | `x²=81` ⇒ **x=±9** |
| B3-2(c) | `12(x+1)²=17−4x` | `12x²+28x−5=0` → `[−28±√1024]/24` → **x=1/6 or −5/2** |
| B3-2(d) | `x+32=(1/7)(x+7)(x−4)` | `7x+224=x²+3x−28` ⇒ `x²−4x−252=0` ⇒ `(x−18)(x+14)=0` ⇒ **x=18 or −14**. Older transcript incorrectly used denominator 5. |

## B3-Q3 One known solution (SOURCE-CORRECTED)

**Original:** x=9 is a solution of `7(x²+3kx+5)=(1−k)x−1`.

(a) Substitute x=9:

`7(81+27k+5)=9(1−k)−1` → `602+189k=8−9k` → `198k=−594` → **k=−3**.

(b) Substitute k=−3:

`7(x²−9x+5)=4x−1` → `7x²−63x+35=4x−1` → `7x²−67x+36=0` → `(x−9)(7x−4)=0` → roots 9 and **4/7**. **Other solution = 4/7.**

> Quality warning: Prior answer k=−34 and 6/7 came from a *different, incorrectly transcribed* equation. Do not include those as B3-Q3 quiz answers.

## B3-Q4 — Hence use substitution

(i) `8x²−35x+12=0` → `8x²−32x−3x+12=0` → `(8x−3)(x−4)=0` ⇒ **x=3/8 or x=4**.

(ii) `8(x+4)²−35(x+4)+12=0`. Set `u=x+4`; from part (i), `u=3/8 or 4` → `x+4=3/8` or `x+4=4` → **x=−29/8 or x=0**.

## B3-Q5 — Three consecutive positive even numbers

Sum of squared numbers = 1208. Let middle number x: `(x−2)²+x²+(x+2)²=1208` → `3x²+8=1208` → `x²=400` → valid x=20 → **18,20,22**. Check `324+400+484=1208`.

## B3-Q6 — Two-digit number

Ones digit is 4 less than tens digit; sum of number and product of digits =56. Let tens=x, ones=x−4: original `11x−4`; product `x(x−4)`. Set `11x−4+x(x−4)=56` → `x²+7x−60=0` → `(x+12)(x−5)=0` → valid tens 5, ones 1, original **51**.

## B3-Q7 — Open-top cuboid

**Original source:** height is 22cm less than length; height is half width; external surface area of five-sided open container =1806cm².

(a) Let length x cm. Height **x−22**; width **2x−44**.

(b) Because top is open: `SA=LW+2LH+2WH=1806`. Insert:

`x(2x−44)+2x(x−22)+2(2x−44)(x−22)=1806`  
`8x²−264x+1936=1806`  
`8x²−264x+130=0`  
**`4x²−132x+65=0`**.

(c) Formula: `x=[132±√(132²−4×4×65)]/(2×4)=[132±128]/8`, roots **32.5** and **0.5**.

(d) Reject x=0.5 because height x−22=−21.5cm is not a possible dimension.

(e) Valid length **32.5cm**, width **21cm**, height **10.5cm**. Volume `32.5×21×10.5` = **7166.25 cm³**.

## B3-Q8 — Quadratic graph and maximum

`y=2−x−0.5x²`, domain `−4≤x≤2`.

| x | −4 | −3 | −2 | −1 | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| y | −2 | 0.5 | 2 | 2.5 | 2 | 0.5 | −2 |

`a=−1/2,b=−1`; `x=−b/(2a)=−1`; `y=2−(−1)−0.5(−1)²=2.5`. **Maximum (−1,2.5)**, line **x=−1**.

# CONTENT 8 — Linear Graphs, Coordinates & Simultaneous Equations

The user's recorded syllabus also includes these curriculum targets (not all have matching question pages in the three Review Exercise PDFs):

- Recognise graphs parallel to coordinate axes: `x=k` and `y=k`; plot `y=x`, `y=−x`.
- Plot linear graphs using x/y tables.
- Midpoint of points `(x₁,y₁),(x₂,y₂)` = `((x₁+x₂)/2,(y₁+y₂)/2)`.
- Calculate gradient `(y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁)` and y-intercept of `y=mx+c`; rearrange `ax+by=c` when b≠0.
- Compare rate of change and y-intercepts; interpret straight-line context, distance–time and conversion graphs.
- Plot two linear equations on common axes; intersection solves simultaneous equations; verify by substitution into *both*.
- Quadratic/linear cross-intersections: for a given quadratic `y=f(x)` and line `y=g(x)`, solve `f(x)=g(x)` to determine x-values; graph solutions can be approximate.

**Existing base-graph method:** keep `y=x²+2x` unchanged and add a comparison line. `x²+2x−3=0`: graph `y=3` intersects at x=−3,1. `x²+3x=0`: graph `y=−x` intersects at x=−3,0.
